title: Resilience Engineering Playbook: Model Inference Lifecycle
author: Evelyn Chen
content:
Summary

This playbook codifies how Redwood’s SRE and runtime teams operate across the model inference lifecycle to preserve customer-facing SLOs while managing cost and capacity. It ties SLO definitions and error budget policy to capacity planning, incident review standards, operational tooling, and concrete runbooks for common failure modes in model-serving (latency spikes, KV cache thrash, OOM cascades, multi-tenant headroom exhaustion).

Purpose and scope

- Purpose: Provide a single, actionable reference that converts SLOs and error budgets into deterministic operational behavior across detection, triage, remediation, and post-incident learning.
- Scope: Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private (customer-managed) deployments for inference runtime. Focus is on production inference services (text generation, chat, embeddings).
- Out of scope: model training pipelines, data labeling workflows, and product UX changes.

Audience

- Primary: SREs, runtime engineers, oncall engineers, incident commanders.
- Secondary: Product owners, capacity planners, solutions engineers, security reviewers.

Key definitions

- SLO: The measurable objective we protect. Example: token-level latency p95 <= 350ms for text-generation API (regional).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; tracked as burn percentage over a rolling 28-day window unless otherwise specified.
- Headroom: Allocated margin above baseline expected utilization used for safe bursts and graceful degradation.
- Burn rate: Rate at which the error budget is consumed vs expected.

SLOs and error budget policy (operational rules)

1) Canonical SLOs (per-model-class, per-region):
   - Availability SLO (request success rate): 99.95% monthly (primary API route).
   - Latency SLOs (generation): p50 <= 50 ms, p95 <= 350 ms, p99 <= 900 ms (short requests, <= 512 tokens).
   - Embedding throughput SLO: 99% of embedding requests served within 200ms for batch size <= 4.

2) Measurement windows and backing metrics:
   - Primary window: rolling 28 days for contractual SLOs, 7 days for fast operational indicators.
   - Metrics: success_rate, latency_p50/p95/p99, token_throughput, cpu_gpu_utilization, kv_cache_hit_rate, queue_depth.

3) Error budget burn policy (automated responses):
   - Low burn (0–10% of budget consumed/week): normal ops.
   - Moderate burn (10–40%/week): investigate trends, run additional traffic mirroring for suspected regressions, increase sampling of slow traces.
   - High burn (40–100%/week): engage oncall escalation, freeze risky rollouts, reduce non-essential background jobs, enable pre-configured capacity hedges.
   - Critical burn (>100% in 24h or >80% week-to-date): declare SLO incident and execute emergency capacity borrowing and graceful degradation policies.

4) Rollout constraints tied to budget: Any candidate runtime change that would risk increasing weekly burn by >10% requires gating via canary with traffic shadowing and rollback window of 60 minutes at the first confirmed p95 regression.

Capacity planning and headroom policy

- Forecast cadence: weekly demand profile refresh for 4-week runway; quarterly capacity planning for 12-month procurement needs.
- Headroom targets (multi-tenant pools): maintain 25% reserved compute headroom for burst absorption for tier-1 customers, 15% for tier-2. Adjust by historic burst factor per model family.
- Elastic reservoir: hold a small pool of ephemeral capacity controlled by SRE for emergency scaling (default reserve = 5% of active fleet per region).
- Preemption and soft-eviction rules:
   1. Non-critical batch jobs (indexing, offline evals) are preempted first.
   2. Dedicated+Private tenant SLAs honored — only hosted best-effort workloads preempted.
   3. When sustained CPU/GPU utilization > 85% for > 10 minutes, trigger autoscale candidate and notify oncall.

Reliability initiatives and exercises

- Quarterly chaos scenarios focusing on: cross-region failover, model hotpatch rollback, KV cache cold-start, and multi-tenant noisy neighbor.
- Pre-release resilience checklist for new model onboarding: warm-pool verification, KV cache sizing, deterministic latency budget tests, and synthetic workload run.
- Resilience radar: maintain a public team board of top-10 failure modes with mitigation status and owners.

Incident review standards and evidence requirements

- Post-incident timeline: initial incident report within 2 hours, draft post-incident review (PIR) within 72 hours, final PIR and action items tracked within 14 days.
- Required evidence for an incident review (minimum):
  - Full timeline of events with UTC timestamps.
  - Alert rules that fired, metric dashboards snapshot (pre/post), and trace samples for slow requests.
  - Heap/GC logs, GPU memory charts, CVM autoscaler events if involved.
  - Runbook steps taken and who executed them.
  - Root-cause hypothesis, confidence level, and planned mitigations.
- PIR structure (template):
  1) Summary and impact (customers, SLO delta).
  2) Timeline.
  3) Root cause & evidence.
  4) Corrective actions (short-term & long-term).
  5) Action owners and due dates.
  6) Post-deployment verification plan.

Operational tooling and automation patterns

- Tooling inventory (recommended):
  - Telemetry: Prometheus (metrics), Tempo (traces), Loki (logs).
  - Alerting: Alertmanager with SLO-linked routing.
  - Runbook automation: Runbook-runner + annotated playbooks in Confluence.
  - Capacity & autoscale control plane: Fleet-orchestrator (internal service), with debounce and safety gates.
  - Canary/shadowing: Traffic-mirroring service integrated with observability.

- Automation patterns to reduce toil:
  1. SLO-driven auto-throttles: when p95 latency > threshold for 5m and error budget burn accelerating, automatically lower non-critical concurrency by 30%.
  2. One-click rollback: policy that ties canary samples to an automated rollback pipeline if latency regressions exceed defined thresholds.
  3. Evidence snapshot automation: on alert, capture dashboard snapshots + trace samples, attach to incident channel.

Runbooks (quick reference)

A) Hotpath triage: sudden latency spike for text-generation route (priority oncall)

1) Initial verification (0–5 minutes):
   - Confirm alert: check Alertmanager and p95 metric.
   - Get impact snapshot: number of affected tokens/minute, per-region spread, any customer escalations.
   - Post status to incident channel with short summary and assign IC.

2) Rapid containment (5–20 minutes):
   - If CPU/GPU utilization > 90%: enable emergency capacity pool (invoke fleet-orchestrator: /api/v1/reserve?pool=emergency&percent=5).
   - If KV cache hit rate dropped > 20%: increase cache size or fall back to cold-path mode with aggressive batching.
   - If model variant rollout ongoing: pause rollout and divert traffic to previous stable variant.

3) Root cause probing (20–60 minutes):
   - Capture representative trace for slow request.
   - Check kernel-level OOMs, CUDA errors in GPU logs, and RPC latency between inference pods and KV store.
   - Run canary traffic to validate mitigation before scaled rollback.

4) Recover and verify (60+ minutes):
   - Confirm p95 back within SLO for two consecutive 5-minute windows.
   - Begin post-incident evidence collection and set PIR timeline.

B) Coldpath remediation: progressive error-rate increase in embedding route (oncall + platform)

1) Verify incidence and scope: compare baseline embedding throughput, queue length, and worker crash logs.
2) Reduce ingestion rate (traffic shaping) for low-priority tenants via rate-limiter service.
3) Redeploy embedding worker with increased batch buffer size and monitor queue drain.

Escalation matrix and ownership

- Tier 1 oncall: initial triage, containment, and short-term mitigations.
- Tier 2: runtime engineers for kernel/quantization issues, model owners for model-level regression investigations.
- SRE Pager lead: incident command if error budget critical or customer-impacting.

Post-incident actions and SLO feedback loop

- For any incident that consumes > 25% of the monthly error budget: require a follow-up capacity plan that includes headroom changes or autoscale parameter adjustments.
- Action item categories: observability gaps, capacity changes, code/regression fixes, runbook updates, and guardrail improvements. Each action must have an owner and a visible target date in the team board.

Sample alert thresholds and response mapping (reference)

| Alert name | Trigger (duration) | Immediate response | Owner |
| Token-latency-p95-high | p95 > 350ms (5m) | Hotpath triage | Oncall Tier 1 |
| Success-rate-drop | success_rate < 99.90% (10m) | Start incident, engage SRE lead | Pager Lead |
| KV-cache-cold | kv_cache_hit_rate < 60% (10m) | Increase cache; enable cold-path | Runtime Team |
| GPU-mem-OOM | OOM count > 1 node (2m) | Isolate node; reassign pods | Infra/SRE |

Autoscaler sample policy (JSON snippet)

{ "autoscale": { "target_gpu_utilization": "70", "scale_up_cooldown_secs": "120", "scale_down_cooldown_secs": "300", "max_scale_step_pct": "30", "safety_headroom_pct": "15" } }

Appendix: verification checklist for model onboarding

- Run 30-minute synthetic traffic run at 2x expected QPS.
- Confirm KV cache hit rate >= 80% within 10 minutes of load.
- Validate p95 latency at expected request sizes and token budgets.
- Observe GPU memory stability for 1,000 synthetic requests.
- Add canary route with 1% production traffic for 48 hours and require no SLO regression.
